description: We are a team of passionate student innovators who believe that meaningful discoveries begin with curiosity and collaboration. United by our interest in technology, artificial intelligence, and Earth observation, we aim to transform complex scientific data into solutions that address real-world challenges.
summary: CSTAR-Energy is a satellite-powered environmental intelligence platform designed to investigate municipal lighting changes and industrial energy transitions. By integrating NASA Black Marble nighttime radiance, Sentinel-5P TROPOMI nitrogen dioxide observations, MERRA-2 meteorological data, and Sentinel-2 land-use information, it examines environmental changes through the proposed Cross-Coupled Transition Fingerprinting (CCTF) framework. The platform provides interactive maps, evidence timelines, atmospheric screening, counterfactual comparisons, and AI-assisted analysis to evaluate possible causes while acknowledging uncertainty. CSTAR-Energy aims to transform complex satellite observations into accessible, evidence-based insights, helping researchers and local governments monitor urban development, prioritize environmental verification, and make informed, sustainable planning decisions for communities.
details:
CSTAR-Energy (Spatiotemporal Radiance & Atmospheric Attribution Platform) is a satellite-powered environmental intelligence and decision-support system designed to monitor nighttime lighting changes, investigate industrial energy transitions, and analyze environmental patterns using Earth observation data and machine learning.

The platform integrates NASA Black Marble nighttime radiance, Sentinel-5P TROPOMI nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) observations, NASA MERRA-2 meteorological data, and Sentinel-2 land-use information. These datasets provide complementary insights into changes in nighttime brightness, atmospheric conditions, wind patterns, and urban development.

Through an interactive web dashboard, users can explore geographic locations, compare historical nighttime radiance observations, identify potential transitions, and investigate supporting environmental evidence.

The system also incorporates machine-learning models for exploratory radiance forecasting. Its spatial Random Forest model predicts nighttime radiance one calendar month ahead and identifies potential brightness increases. Evaluated on 180,000 chronological cell-month test samples, the model achieved 71.89% directional accuracy, a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.1168, and an ROC AUC of 0.7501. However, its precision of 17.80% indicates that predicted increases may include a substantial number of false positives.

Additionally, the platform introduces the proposed Cross-Coupled Transition Fingerprinting (CCTF) framework, which organizes radiance trends, atmospheric observations, meteorological conditions, geographic context, and historical evidence to assess possible explanations for environmental changes. Its current mechanism scores are illustrative rather than scientifically validated causal conclusions.


The platform provides a centralized environment for exploring satellite observations and organizing environmental investigations. Its primary benefits include simplifying complex Earth observation data through interactive maps and visualizations, identifying locations that may require further investigation, and supporting comparisons between nighttime lighting and atmospheric changes.

It also helps researchers evaluate available evidence, recognize missing or insufficient observations, and distinguish preliminary predictions from verified findings.

By using publicly available Earth observation datasets, the system offers a potentially accessible approach for communities and institutions with limited resources for environmental monitoring.


The project aims to support researchers, environmental organizations, urban planners, and local government units in making informed decisions about urban development, infrastructure modernization, and industrial activity.

It seeks to improve environmental awareness by identifying potential changes in nighttime lighting and atmospheric conditions that might otherwise receive limited attention.

For local governments, the platform could help prioritize areas for field verification, support infrastructure assessments, and provide additional evidence for environmental planning.

Its long-term vision is to make satellite-based environmental intelligence more accessible, transparent, and scientifically responsible, contributing to sustainable urban development and improved environmental monitoring.


The system was developed as a web-based research platform using a modular software architecture. Its documented development technologies and components include:

  • Python: Used for satellite data processing, analytical workflows, feature engineering, and machine-learning development.
  • FastAPI: Used for backend services, API endpoints, and communication between the analytical modules and dashboard.
  • React and TypeScript: Used to develop the interactive frontend dashboard, including its monitoring, investigation, and visualization interfaces.
  • PostgreSQL and PostGIS: Included in the planned architecture for managing structured records, geospatial information, observation metadata, and analytical outputs.
  • Random Forest: Used for exploratory nighttime radiance forecasting and brightness-increase classification.
  • Regional multimodal modeling: Used to investigate monthly radiance patterns through a separate experimental evaluation.
  • Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network (ST-GNN): A proposed experimental component for investigating spatial and temporal relationships.
  • NASA Black Marble, NASA MERRA-2, Sentinel-5P TROPOMI, and Sentinel-2: Earth observation data sources supporting the research workflow.
  • Git and GitHub: Used for source-code management and team collaboration.

The system is designed to operate on standard computing hardware and does not require dedicated physical environmental sensors or custom satellite equipment.


The project's innovation lies in moving beyond conventional nighttime satellite maps toward an integrated environmental investigation platform.

Instead of simply displaying whether an area becomes brighter or darker, it combines nighttime radiance, atmospheric nitrogen dioxide, meteorological observations, geographic information, and machine-learning predictions to examine possible explanations for environmental transitions.

Its proposed Cross-Coupled Transition Fingerprinting framework introduces an event-centered approach that considers multiple evidence categories rather than relying on a single measurement.

Another distinctive feature is the integration of interactive nighttime-light maps, historical evidence timelines, source–plume screening, counterfactual comparisons, and structured transition assessments within a single research environment.

The platform also emphasizes uncertainty-aware analysis. Rather than automatically assigning a definitive explanation, its framework allows events to remain unresolved when the available evidence is incomplete or contradictory.

This combination of multi-sensor analysis, exploratory artificial intelligence, and transparent evidence review represents its proposed contribution to environmental decision-support technology.


Our team considered several important factors to ensure that the platform would be technically feasible, scientifically responsible, and useful to its intended users.

Data availability and quality: We considered the accessibility, completeness, temporal coverage, and reliability of satellite observations. The dashboard tracks dataset readiness, with three of five listed datasets currently marked as Ready.

Scientific accuracy: We recognized that nighttime brightness does not directly measure electricity consumption and that atmospheric NO₂ observations cannot independently establish industrial responsibility or emissions reductions.

Spatial and temporal differences: Because satellite instruments have different observation times and geographic resolutions, the system's analytical design emphasizes appropriate data alignment while preserving the limitations of the original measurements.

Machine-learning performance: We evaluated predictive performance using error measurements and classification metrics, including MAE, RMSE, accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and ROC AUC. We also considered false-positive predictions and the limitations of small evaluation datasets.

Uncertainty and transparency: We designed the research workflow to distinguish actual observations, exploratory predictions, synthetic demonstrations, and interpretations requiring further verification.

Usability and accessibility: We prioritized a clean, interactive dashboard with understandable visualizations, organized evidence panels, and accessible navigation to help users explore complex environmental information.

Scalability and future development: We considered a modular system architecture, additional geographic coverage, expanded historical datasets, improved machine-learning evaluation, and integration with independently verified environmental records.

Environmental and community relevance: We focused on how satellite observations could support practical research and local decision-making without overstating their ability to prove environmental impacts.


By combining NASA and partner Earth observation datasets with exploratory machine learning and an evidence-centered analytical framework, CSTAR-Energy provides a foundation for identifying potential nighttime lighting and industrial transitions while communicating uncertainty and encouraging independent verification.

The project demonstrates how satellite observations and interactive visualization can support environmental investigations and contribute to more informed decision-making.

Our goal is not simply to detect changes from space, but to help communities understand the evidence behind those changes and make better-informed decisions for a more sustainable future
